header:
Problem 4 Rotaxane Actuators and Mechanochemistry (28 points, 12%)
In the 38th Preliminary Round, we encountered the following reaction. Its principle is to apply mechanical force to a molecule so that four four-membered rings open sequentially: [Image: Exam-22-T4-header-1.png]
Mechanical force can do more than break covalent bonds: changing the force direction and mode of molecular deformation can select the reaction pathway. In 2024, Chen and co-workers constructed a rotaxane mechanical actuator using the sliding motion of a pillar[5]arene macrocycle relative to the axle. Mechanical action transmitted by ultrasonic cavitation allows the macrocycle to push mechanically responsive cargo sites along the axle and release the cargo molecules sequentially.

header_images.description: On the left is the structure of a polymer whose repeating-unit fragment has SMILES '[*]=CC1C(C2C3C4C=CC4C3C21)C=[*]'; the units are connected to one another through double bonds. On the right is a horizontal arrow pointing right, labeled “ultrasound, THF, 6~9 °C, Ar”.

subquestions.text_open:
4.1 Synthesis of a rotaxane requires threading and end-capping. After threading, repeated sequences of dethreading → rethreading → dethreading may occur before end-capping is completed. In this study, the rotaxane structure was constructed by the reaction below. Threading can occur in two orientations, forming products in which the pillar[5]arene macrocycle and the 2-bromo-2-methylpropanoyloxy group on the axle lie on opposite sides (A$_{trans}$) or the same side (A$_{cis}$).
Based on the reaction information above, write the SMILES string for B.

text_images.description: Rotaxane construction scheme. The reactants are 'COC(C=C(C(OC)=C1)CC2=C(C=C(C(OC)=C2)CC3=C(C=C(C(OC)=C3)CC4=C(C=C5C(OC)=C4)OC)OC)OC)=C1CC6=C(C=C(C(OC)=C6)C5)OCOC(C(Br)(C)C)=O' and 'CC(C)(Br)C(OCCCCCCCCCCCCO)=O'. Under BTBSCl, Et3N, CHCl3, -15 °C, 2 h, the products are [A$_{trans}$] (11%), [A$_{cis}$] (13%), and [B] (69%). The structure of the end-capping reagent BTBSCl, 'ClS(C1=CC(C(F)(F)F)=CC(C(F)(F)F)=C1)(=O)=O', is also shown. The structures of A$_{trans}$, A$_{cis}$, and B are not drawn; only their labels and yields are given.

rubric: The SMILES of B is 'CC(C)(Br)C(OCCCCCCCCCCCCOS(C1=CC(C(F)(F)F)=CC(C(F)(F)F)=C1)(=O)=O)=O' (3 points).

subquestions.text_open:
4.2.3 In addition to the cis/trans stereoisomerism caused by the orientation of the long PMA polymer chains in the rotaxane, the [4+2] adduct fragment in the cargo molecule also exhibits endo/exo stereoisomerism. Using $^1$H NMR, the researchers measured the conversion of the Diels–Alder adduct, i.e., the cargo-release efficiency, for the four molecules and obtained the following data:

| Species | cis-endo | cis-exo | trans-endo | trans-exo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cargo released/% | 62 | 51 | 71 | 71 |

Under the experimental conditions, the long PMA polymer chains experience mechanical forces from the extensional flow field generated by ultrasonic cavitation, causing the pillar[5]arene macrocycle to slide along the axle. Based on the data above, determine the force direction on the polymer chain attached to the pillar[5]arene macrocycle, either from the chain terminus toward the pillar[5]arene macrocycle or from the pillar[5]arene macrocycle toward the chain terminus, and briefly explain your answer.
rubric: From the pillar[5]arene macrocycle toward the chain terminus. (2 points) The data show that for both endo and exo adducts, the trans rotaxane has a higher release efficiency than the corresponding cis rotaxane. (1 point) This indicates that pulling the two PMA chains apart in opposite directions, as in the trans configuration, more effectively activates the cargo site. (1 point) Therefore, the force direction is from the pillar[5]arene macrocycle toward the chain terminus.

subquestions.text_open:
4.3 In addition, a cargo-bearing chain can carry multiple cargo molecules to form an oligomeric cargo chain. The pillar[5]arene macrocycle can then move continuously along the main axle and release cargo from multiple cargo sites in sequence by a “pushing” action from front to back. Researchers developed rotaxane compounds containing 3 cargo units ($n$ = 0 in the figure below) and 5 cargo units ($n$ = 1 in the figure below), as shown:
4.3.2 The researchers found, however, that increasing the number of cargo molecules loaded into a rotaxane markedly decreased the release efficiency. Rotaxanes carrying 3 or 5 cargo molecules released fewer than 2 cargo molecules on average. For this calculation, the rotaxane composed of the pillar[5]arene macrocycle and axle is treated as one molecule.

| Number of cargo molecules loaded | Average release per site/% | Internal-site release/% | Terminal-site release/% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 71 | / | / |
| 3 | 44 | 45 | 42 |
| 5 | 22 | 22 | 23 |

Based on these data, propose one reasonable explanation for the decrease in release efficiency.

text_images.description: The figure shows a supramolecular assembly. One component is a pillar[5]arene with structure 'COC1=C(CC2=C(O[R])C=C(C3)C(OC)=C2)C=C(OC)C(CC4=C(OC)C=C(CC5=C(OC)C=C(CC6=C(OC)C=C3C(OC)=C6)C(OC)=C5)C(OC)=C4)=C1'. The guest is a polymeric structure with repeating units and has SMILES '[R]OCCCCCCCCCCCCOC(C1=CC=CC(OCCN2N=NC(CCCCOC[C@@]3(O4)C=C[C@@]4(COCCCCC5=CN(CCCCCCOC[C@@]6(O7)C=C[C@@]7(COCCCCCCN8N=NC(CCCCOC[C@@]9%10C=C[C@@](O%10)(OCCCCC%11=CN(CCCCCCOC[C@@]%12(O%13)C=C[C@@]%13(COCCCCCCN%14C=C(CCCCOC[C@@]%15%16C=C[C@H](O%16)C(C(N%17C(C%18=CC=CC=C%18)(C%19=CC=CC=C%19)C%20=CC=CC=C%20)=O)C%15C%17=O)N=N%14)C(C(N%21C(C%22=CC=CC=C%22)(C%23=CC=CC=C%23)C%24=CC=CC=C%24)=O)C%12C%21=O)N=N%11)C(C(N%25C(C%26=CC=CC=C%26)(C%27=CC=CC=C%27)C%28=CC=CC=C%28)=O)C9C%25=O)=C8)C(C(N%29C(C%30=CC=CC=C%30)(C%31=CC=CC=C%31)C%32=CC=CC=C%32)=O)C6C%29=O)N=N5)C(C(N%33C(C%34=CC=CC=C%34)(C%35=CC=CC=C%35)C%36=CC=CC=C%36)=O)C3C%33=O)=C2)=C1)=O'. The repeating-unit fragment has structure 'O=C1N(C(C2=CC=CC=C2)(C3=CC=CC=C3)C4=CC=CC=C4)C(C(C51)[C@](O6)(OCCCCC7=CN(CCCCCCOC[C@@]8(O9)C=C[C@@]9(COCCCCCCN%10C=C(CCCC[*])N=N%10)C(C(N%11C(C%12=CC=CC=C%12)(C%13=CC=CC=C%13)C%14=CC=CC=C%14)=O)C8C%11=O)N=N7)C=C[C@]56CO[*])=O'. The R groups on the pillar[5]arene and guest are polymer chains whose SMILES may be represented as '[*]C(C(C)(C)CC(C(OC)=O)Br)=O', where * is the attachment point to another group. The repeating unit of R is '[*]CC(C(OC)=O)[*]', where * marks connections between repeat units.

rubric: The long PMA chains may break under ultrasound and thus fail to drive the pillar[5]arene along the axle. (2 points; any answer involving chain breakage is accepted, such as breakage of the cargo chain preventing some rotaxanes from releasing cargo.) Consequently, some rotaxanes cannot release cargo, whereas others release cargo from nearly all sites. (2 points) No credit is given for stating that the pillar[5]arene macrocycle slips off the axle.

subquestions.text_open:
4.4 In addition to cargo release driven by a “pushing” action, the researchers designed the molecule below to investigate the effect of a “pulling” action on cargo release.
Under ultrasound in aqueous solution, the molecule undergoes not only a retro-[4+2] reaction but also heterolytic C-N bond cleavage to give two additional products.
4.4.1 Write the SMILES strings for the two products formed by heterolytic C-N bond cleavage, both of which contain long polymer chains.

text_images.description: The molecule used to study the “pulling” action has SMILES 'O=C1N(C(C2=CC=CC=C2)(C3=CC=C(OCC4=CN(CCCO[R])N=N4)C=C3)C5=CC=CC=C5)C([C@@]6([H])[C@]7(COC(C)=O)C=C[C@](O7)(CCCCCC8=CN(N=N8)CCCO[R])[C@]61[H])=O'. [R] is a placeholder for a PMA polymer chain, and both side chains are -CH2CH2CH2-O-[R]. The definition of R is also shown at the left: R = ~C(=O)C(CH3)2CH2CH(Br)(CH2)mCO2Me, where ~ is the connection point and m is a subscript.

rubric: (2 points each; the order may be reversed, and drawing the R substituents explicitly is also accepted)

The left product has SMILES 'O=C1NC([C@@]2([H])[C@]3(COC(C)=O)C=C[C@](O3)(CCCCCC4=CN(N=N4)CCCO[R])[C@]21[H])=O'. The right product has SMILES 'OC(C1=CC=CC=C1)(C2=CC=C(OCC3=CN(CCCO[R])N=N3)C=C2)C4=CC=CC=C4'. Both products contain the [R] placeholder for a PMA chain.
